question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• A roundabout is a circular intersection where drivers yield to traffic already inside and travel in one direction around a central island.
• In 2019, the city of Delmar Falls replaced the traffic signal at Pike Street and Ninth Avenue with a single-lane roundabout.
• In the five years before the change, the intersection averaged 11 injury crashes per year; in the five years after, it averaged 3.
• Daily traffic through the intersection was about 14,000 vehicles both before and after the change.
• Drivers entering a roundabout typically slow to 15 to 20 miles per hour, compared with the higher speeds common when passing through a green light.
• The Pike Street roundabout cost $1.4 million to build, about three times the cost of a typical signal upgrade, and its central island is planted with native grasses.

The student wants to support the general claim that roundabouts can make intersections safer by presenting a specific example to an audience that is skeptical of the claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Drivers entering a roundabout typically slow to 15 to 20 miles per hour, which is well below the higher speeds common when drivers pass through an intersection on a green light.
answer_b: In 2019, Delmar Falls replaced the traffic signal at Pike Street and Ninth Avenue with a single-lane roundabout, and in the five years afterward the intersection averaged 3 injury crashes per year.
answer_c: At Pike Street and Ninth Avenue in Delmar Falls, injury crashes fell from 11 per year to 3 after a roundabout replaced a signal, while daily traffic held steady near 14,000 vehicles.
answer_d: The Pike Street roundabout in Delmar Falls cost $1.4 million to build, about three times the cost of a typical signal upgrade, and its central island is planted with native grasses.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it supports the general claim with a specific example from the notes and anticipates a skeptic's objection. It gives a concrete location (Pike Street and Ninth Avenue in Delmar Falls), the before-and-after crash figures (11 per year to 3), and the note that daily traffic stayed near 14,000 vehicles, which counters the doubt that the drop was caused by fewer cars rather than by the roundabout.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It states a true general fact about driver speeds in roundabouts, but it is not a specific example and offers no evidence that any real intersection became safer, so it does not meet the goal of presenting an example for a skeptical audience.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It gives the specific location and the after-change crash average, but it omits the earlier average of 11 crashes per year, so a skeptical reader has no basis for comparison and cannot see that safety improved.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It draws on a note about construction cost and landscaping, which relates to a different claim (about expense or appearance) and provides no evidence about safety.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Researchers at Alderwick University studied whether a ten-minute outdoor walk before brainstorming affects creative output.
• The study included 48 undergraduates, all recruited from a single introductory psychology course.
• Students who walked outdoors generated an average of 14 uses for a common object, compared with an average of 10 for students who sat indoors.
• The walk took place on a tree-lined campus path in the spring.
• Two independent raters, who agreed closely with each other, scored the students' ideas.
• The researchers wrote that the results should be considered preliminary and may not apply to other age groups or settings.

The student wants to report the study's main finding while making clear its limitation for an audience that needs an accurate sense of how far the results can be trusted. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: At Alderwick University, students who took a ten-minute outdoor walk before brainstorming generated an average of 14 uses for a common object, compared with 10 for students who sat indoors, showing that walking boosts creativity.
answer_b: Because students who walked outdoors averaged 14 uses for a common object while seated students averaged 10, the researchers concluded that a short walk improves brainstorming for people of any age in any setting.
answer_c: To measure creative output, researchers at Alderwick University had 48 undergraduates brainstorm after a ten-minute walk on a tree-lined campus path in spring, and two independent raters who agreed closely scored their ideas.
answer_d: In a study of 48 undergraduates from one psychology course, those who took a ten-minute outdoor walk averaged 14 uses for a common object versus 10 for seated students, though the researchers called the results preliminary.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it states the study's main finding (walkers averaged 14 uses for a common object versus 10 for seated students) and also conveys the limitation: the sample was 48 undergraduates from a single psychology course, and the researchers themselves called the results preliminary. This gives an audience that needs accuracy both the result and a basis for judging how far it can be trusted.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It presents the finding accurately but omits the limitation, and the phrase "showing that walking boosts creativity" overstates what a small, preliminary study of one group can establish.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It states the finding but overgeneralizes: the notes say the results may not apply to other age groups or settings, so claiming the researchers concluded the walk helps people of any age in any setting contradicts the notes.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It draws on details about the method (the campus path, the season, the raters) that are not relevant to the goal, and it never states the finding or the researchers' qualification of it.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Bartolomeo Cristofori was born in Padua, Italy, in 1655.
• Around 1688, he moved to Florence to build and maintain instruments for Prince Ferdinando de' Medici.
• Cristofori is credited with inventing the piano around 1700.
• Earlier keyboard instruments, such as the harpsichord, sound by plucking strings, so a player cannot change a note's loudness by touch.
• Cristofori's hammer mechanism lets a player make notes louder or softer by changing how hard a key is pressed.
• Only three of his pianos, all made in the 1720s, are known to survive today.

The student wants to emphasize the significance of Cristofori's contribution to museum visitors who are about to view one of his surviving pianos. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Cristofori's hammer mechanism let players vary a note's loudness by how hard they pressed a key, something that plucked-string harpsichords could not do.
answer_b: Born in Padua in 1655, Cristofori moved to Florence around 1688, where he built and maintained instruments for Prince Ferdinando de' Medici, a member of the Medici family.
answer_c: Because only three of Cristofori's pianos, all made in the 1720s, are known to survive today, visitors are fortunate to be able to see one of these rare instruments in person.
answer_d: Cristofori, who is credited with inventing the piano around 1700, built and maintained instruments in Florence for Prince Ferdinando de' Medici, who employed him there.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it explains why Cristofori's work matters to visitors. The notes state that harpsichords pluck strings, so players cannot change loudness by touch, while Cristofori's hammer mechanism lets a player make notes louder or softer by how hard a key is pressed. Combining these two notes shows what the piano allowed that earlier keyboard instruments did not, which conveys the significance of his contribution.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It gives true biographical facts (his birth year, birthplace, and move to Florence), but these details do not convey why his contribution was significant.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The rarity of his surviving pianos is accurate and may interest visitors, but it concerns the scarcity of the objects, not the significance of what Cristofori contributed.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It mentions the invention of the piano but omits what made the invention important, such as the hammer mechanism and the control over loudness. It instead emphasizes his employer and the setting, which are biographical details.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Wexley Mill Museum occupies a restored 1880s flour mill in the town of Wexley.
• Its top-floor gallery displays more than 300 historic tools donated by local families.
• On the first Sunday of each month, admission to the museum is free for all visitors.
• In the museum's Water Wheel Room, visitors can operate a working miniature water wheel and a set of grinding stones.
• The museum's ground-floor archive holds deed records dating to 1851 and is open by appointment only.
• Guided tours for school groups must be reserved at least two weeks in advance.

The student wants to persuade local families with young children to visit the museum. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Anyone curious about Wexley's past can browse the top-floor gallery of more than 300 historic tools donated by local families and then request an appointment to read deed records dating to 1851.
answer_b: Families with young children can visit the Wexley Mill Museum, a restored 1880s flour mill, free of charge on the first Sunday of each month and tour its top-floor gallery of historic tools.
answer_c: Teachers who want students to try a working miniature water wheel and grinding stones should reserve a guided school tour at least two weeks before the date of their planned visit.
answer_d: Families with young children can visit the Wexley Mill Museum for free on the first Sunday of any month and work a miniature water wheel and grinding stones themselves.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it accomplishes the stated goal of persuading families with young children to visit by pairing a practical detail with an appealing detail. The notes state that admission is free on the first Sunday of each month, which gives families a practical reason to go on a specific day. The notes also state that visitors can operate a working miniature water wheel and grinding stones, a hands-on experience likely to appeal to families with young children.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It uses details about the tool gallery and the deed records, which would interest people researching local history rather than families with young children, and it includes no detail about cost or timing that would help families decide when to visit.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It gives a practical detail, free admission on the first Sunday of each month, but its only appealing detail is a gallery of historic tools. It omits the hands-on Water Wheel Room, which is the feature most likely to attract families with young children.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It mentions the hands-on water wheel and grinding stones, but it pairs them with the school-tour reservation requirement, which matters to teachers, not to families with young children deciding when to visit.
